analysis.one_liner: Strips the National Labor Relations Board of its power to prosecute workplace law violations.
analysis.headline: A bill to strip most enforcement power from the National Labor Relations Board died in a Senate committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the National Labor Relations Act so the NLRB could only investigate allegations of employer misconduct — firing workers for organizing, interfering with elections, breaking contracts — but not prosecute them, issue binding orders, ask courts to enforce its decisions, or seek injunctions. Instead of the agency handling a complaint, a worker would have to file their own federal lawsuit against their employer. The Board would also be barred from writing rules affecting anyone's rights, and forced to review and rescind its existing regulations. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers — especially those accused of firing workers for union activity, interfering with organizing drives, or manipulating representation elections — would gain the most. Today, an employer facing an NLRB complaint gets a free prosecution, a decision, and a court-enforced order; under this bill, the worker would instead have to fund and litigate a federal lawsuit alone. Companies that want to avoid unionization would face far less risk of meaningful consequences.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers accused of labor law violations

how_it_helps.text: It removes the NLRB's power to issue and prosecute unfair labor practice complaints, replacing prosecution with a civil action the aggrieved worker or union would have to bring themselves in federal district court.
It limits the Board's rulemaking to its own internal procedures, barring any rule affecting the rights of employers, employees, or unions, and requires rescinding existing regulations to comply.
It repeals the Board's authority to issue orders preventing unfair labor practices, seek injunctions, or have courts enforce its orders, leaving only the power to investigate.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who lose their jobs or are otherwise harmed by employer misconduct would bear the cost: no agency to prosecute their case, no binding order, no injunction, and the burden of suing a better-resourced employer in federal court. Labor unions would lose the enforcement framework that underpins organizing and elections.

drawbacks.text: Workers alleging illegal firings or union-busting would have to sue employers themselves in federal court instead of having the NLRB prosecute for them, a cost and legal burden most individual employees cannot easily bear.
The bill repeals the NLRB's authority to seek court enforcement of its orders and to seek injunctions, so even a ruling in a worker's favor could not be enforced by the agency.

The Board would be barred from issuing rules affecting any substantive or procedural rights of employers, employees, or unions — including rules on representation elections — and would have to review and revise or rescind its existing regulations within six months.
The Board loses authority to hold hearings on jurisdictional strikes, a tool that has historically kept disputes between unions from shutting down workplaces.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's only real benefit is reducing what its supporters see as regulatory overreach by an independent agency, moving disputes from a specialized labor tribunal to individual lawsuits and general courts. The costs fall on workers: the complaint system would no longer prosecute violations, injunctions against unlawful firings would end, and enforcement of orders would disappear. Individual civil suits are a poor substitute — ordinary employees rarely have the money or legal help to take an employer to federal court. On balance, the drawbacks dominate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2021 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 117th Congress: no hearing, no committee markup, and no vote ever occurred.
Had it become law, it would have replaced NLRB prosecution of unfair labor practices with private civil lawsuits and stripped the Board's authority to issue orders or seek court enforcement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who violate workers' rights are better off: with the bill dead, the NLRB's powers to prosecute complaints, issue orders, and enforce them in court were never taken away.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the NLRB of its complaint, rulemaking, and enforcement powers.

for.name: Sens. Marsha Blackburn, Mike Braun, and Rand Paul

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican support — one sponsor and three cosponsors out of 50 Senate Republicans — and never attracted a Democratic cosponsor.

industries.note: Employers accused of illegal firings, retaliation, or blocking union elections would face a toothless investigator instead of a prosecutor and court-enforceable orders, dramatically lowering the risk and cost of violating labor law.

industries.industry: Anti-union employers and management-side law firms
industries.note: Replacing free agency-run complaint prosecution with individual federal lawsuits shifts disputes to venues where employers hold the resource advantage, and firms that specialize in defeating union efforts gain business.
Unions would lose the agency that polices employer interference in organizing and elections, making it harder to represent members and organize new workplaces.
